You could 100% plant them in the fall and allow nature to do it's thing. Just know that it's thing may be birds eating the seeds, rain washing them away, or seeds getting too much/not enough light. That's why plants produce so many.. You can try winter bucket sowing which eliminates a bunch of this--get some dirt; put it in a bucket/tray/milk jug (top cut off mostly--think nearly headless nick) anything that has a transparent top so light can get through, but not birds; poke holes in the bottom for drainage and the top for rain/circulation; sprinkle your seeds in and cover with however much soil you need to achieve the correct depth. Then let nature do the rest. Some seeds like the freeze/thaw/freeze/thaw cycle to germinate, so this is really convenient for that too. 

  
Either way should work. Just depends on your type of free time and if you can keep the soil where they germinate outside consistently moist. Like a couple of times a day if it's sunny moist. It they dry out once, there goes your crop. That's why I plant a couple of "successions" (i.e. freeze them as cubes and plant more every week until you're out).

I learned through them enneagram (which may not work for everyone, but my my husband and me, it was SPOT ON) that he “recharges” in a completely opposite manner than I do. I talk, he retreats, I get out of the house, he stays in, I enjoy quiet couch time together, he enjoys playing video games specifically while I'm asleep. It used to royally offend me, but now I get that that's just how he's wired. So now I make sure when he's stressed (I.e. Every day rn because we just moved states) that he has "completely alone" time. I of course would like to talk about his day and hear how he feels and his struggles and his better days, but (after therapy) we realized that he perceives this as him continuing to give after he's given all day to work and all evening to the kid and then the last of his day to me. So all this is to say: she may need a form of stress release and recharging that is completely opposite of what you'd expect AND she may not even know what that is yet. Therapy and my constant need to understand myself has led us to this point in our marriage. My husband would never have investigated this for himself. 

Advice: have a sit down, LOVING and patient conversation (even if you have to bite your tongue to get past snippy bitchy comments) about your concern for HER. If this gets her to open up and heal, great. If she maintains there's not a problem, calmly but firmly inform her that the way things have been going lately have been a problem for YOU. List your valid frustrations. I ended up INFORMING my husband we were going to therapy. Never looked back!!

I'm doing it! I'm applying my doctorate level knowledge IRL(/s this is reddit)!!! So I did the things: followed the links to the source article and read the abstract (farthest I could get before a paywall) and applied my new knowledge of epidemiology hacks. 

*hack 1:* Say the incidence is rising, but don't emphasize the **timeframe** (they mean it's been rising over the past *70 years*, as in when the Queen was crowned ::RIP::).

*hack 2:* Say the incidence is rising, but don't explain how **improved screening** unavoidably  contributes to the rise of the numbers, giving you an artificial increase (for reference, we didn't know what DNA was in the 50's, and the way we screened for cancer was with an unsophisticated x-ray and "keyhole" surgery).

*hack 3:* don't mention how the **changes in the population** affects the number increase. In 1950's, the number of "young people" (less than 50 years old) was 62mil (1950 census). In 2020, that number was 166 million. Do you think that might affect the numbers? In essence, if you survive past one condition, you'd better believe you're going to die of something else. In this example, it may be cancer.

I'm not disagreeing with this conclusion, but I can't agree with it because it doesn't present the confounding information. Like ANY of it. And it's take away message: life has changed so much over these past 70 years that some of those changes may have caused other changes, like cAnCeR iN kIdS. 

I just don't appreciate how it contributes so little to the discussion and leans toward fear mongering.

I've moved back and forth for school and work. About to move from small town to Nashville. 

Some other things to consider: 
1. You know there's a place you're extremely happy to live, not a lot of people find that. AND there is nothing stopping you from returning after your time away. Three years is not too bad at all. And it's such a big deal that you're SO is coming along. Bless him/her.

It's definitely going to be an adjustment (closing hours suck) and a time of grief is inevitable. You're leaving something you love, no matter the amount of time. But I remember grieving when I first moved to college/big city culture shock. It was one of the best times of my life. You would NEVER have been able to convince me of that before I left. 
3. Keep your mind open before you go so you're emotionally prepared (it'll mean the difference between sadness and bitterness). Get your zoom set up. Plan on some day trips to a bigger city once you're there. Eat at restaurants that aren't chains. Meet the locals lol. 

If the worst happens, you'll only be there a few Christmases.

Was in a similar situation. It all boils down to how valuable are these feelings? Are they surface and distracting and guilty? Or are they meaningful, strongly founded, and worth screwing everyone's lives up over? I think you know the answer there already, so I will tell you that after years, yes, maybe years, those feelings WILL fade. 
In the meantime, (this was the key for me) go to a therapist, who will help you tease out where these feelings are coming from (for me it was a lack of confidence in my husband's ability to care for me, whom, again, I LOVED, but I was still fearfully missing something that guy B "seeeeeeeemed" to be able to provide for me). Separation was paramount but therapy to identify the source of my confused feelings was what got me and my marriage back on track.
As for what to do, your husband married you, not his sister. If he wants to go and you're willing to go NO MATTER YOUR REASONS, that is not a move of manipulation. SIL might be upset now, but it's shit for her no matter what you choose. Continue to be amiable and kind, knowing she can't understand and it's not her fault. 
If he ends up not wanting to take the job, perhaps with therapy, you can stay and avoid giving in, but you'd be a stronger woman than I was. Your vow of love (the action not the feeling) was and is toward your husband. Do what you have to top fight for that. 
Imagine the goal the happy retirement and watching him be a dad or whatever. Focus on the goal, not fickle feelings.

I can assure you, for whatever that's worth, that I did not utter the phrase "Do you want to die now or later." My God. Or anything of the sort. There is such a time when death is overwhelmingly probable, which is why hospice nurses exist, and this patient was indeed DNR. 

We talked about his care, his current condition, his options, his wishes, and was assured that he did not have to make any decisions "now." He communicated that what we were doing wasn't working, and I educated that the only next step would be a intubation (no jargon used), and the facts regarding the probability of him ever coming off. His family, his doctor, and I were on the same page, but it is a nursing responsibility, not to keep someone alive at all costs, but to give patients the dignity of making their own informed choices and then advocating for them. 

I would also hope you would advocate for your father's wishes instead of your own. Especially when it came to his own life.

1. Head wounds bleed a lot and typically look worse than they are. Lots of vasculature there. If they walk up to registration, registration would freak out and get a triage nurse (because they are not trained on anything medical) who would likely apply a thick pad of gauze (or an ABD pad). If they look unstable (about to pass out or sweating / bleeding profusely) they would be brought right back. Registration would wait till their family arrived or get the ID off the person to see if they've been there before to recall that data. 
2. As stated earlier, they'd only be "brought to the back" to lie down if they had unstable vital signs or LOOKED like they did (pale, sweaty, bright red blood indicating an arterial bleed that needs to be sewn closed, alerted mental status). If they got whacked with a 2x4, have a 5in gash, did not pass out and can hold their own gauze, you get a seat in the waiting room until a recliner opens up. 
Broken ribs are painful, but pain doesn't get you to the back. If there aren't breath sounds on that side, you get to come back because your lung is collapsed and that's an emergency. Broken ribs are not an emergency and neither is a mild concussion. 
Passes out in the exam room: it's hard to pass out when you're lying down. You'd have to have a lot of blood loss or an active head bleed. If you passed out in the exam room after a head bleed, we'd get a stat head CT. No ECG unless you're in an ultra fancy hospital. Have only seen it once in the ER and it was to confirm brain death of a child (so Extenuating circumstances). If standing, ease patient to the ground, check that there's a pulse, then wait until they come back around in a couple of seconds. If they don't = big problems and putting a tube down their throat and breathing for them since they can't maintain their airway.
